title: Hosted API concurrent-hedge flood field journal
content:
Summary:
This document is a field journal-style postmortem and runbook-draft capturing the P0 outage on 2026-05-28 where hosted API saw a sudden p99/p999 latency spiral and partial streaming fragmentation. Impact was concentrated across the east-1 region for ~23 minutes with elevated 5xx and client reconnects. This note mixes on-call observations, timeline, root-cause hypotheses, short-term mitigations executed by responders, and medium-term runbook/experiments to prevent recurrence.

High-level impact:
- Window: 2026-05-28 17:41 - 18:04 UTC (23 minutes)
- Symptoms: p99 latency increased from ~450ms -> 5.1s; streaming sessions saw partial fragmentation and forced reconnects; elevated 5xx rate (1.8% -> 9.6%) on multiplexed edge proxies
- Customer visible: timeouts on chat streaming, client reconnects, increased user perceived truncation in long responses
- Affected surface: hosted API edge -> multiplexing proxies -> ephemeral multiplexer -> serving runtime for gpt-weights-v2 family

Initial on-call notes (raw):
- Pager fired for p99-latency-east-1 and 5xx-spike-multiplexed-edge.
- First 7 minutes: telemetry showed a steady increase in concurrent hedges (hedge requests triggered due to slow-returning model shards).
- Edge counters: active streams spiked while ephemeral pool headroom shrank -> acceptor backlog grew.
- Autoscaler didn’t add capacity; decision signal suppressed because node-level mem/cpu looked healthy (false negative due to metric cardinality aggregation).
- Several legacy clients opened long-lived multiplexed sessions that were sending many small requests (high rps-per-connection).

Timeline (constructed):
- 17:40:30 UTC - small surge of requests from a partner integration (identified later as partner-bETA). Concurrency per connection increased x6.
- 17:41:05 UTC - first alert: p99-latency-east-1 crossing threshold.
- 17:41:30 UTC - oncall started triage; streaming dashboard shows growing ack latency and acceptor backlog.
- 17:42:10 UTC - fencing rule kicked for one edge node; hedges amplify due to partial request duplication -> more in-flight tokens.
- 17:43:17 UTC - autoscaler did not trigger to add more serving instances; investigation shows group-level metric used for scaling aggregated away per-session hotness.
- 17:45:00 UTC - responders applied targeted ratecap on partner-bETA token group via quota override (manual throttle) which reduced new hedges.
- 17:47:30 UTC - short-term mitigation: adjusted hedging multiplier to lower parallel hedges for streaming path (rollbackable change).
- 17:52:00 UTC - streaming fragmentation decreased, p99 trending down slowly.
- 18:03:50 UTC - metrics back to baseline; alerts closed after 2 stable windows.

Root cause analysis (hypotheses validated):
1) Interaction of hedging policy + per-connection high RPS clients: hedging triggers duplicated requests when initial shard responses delayed -> multiplicative in-flight work (validated by traces showing duplicated request IDs).
2) Autoscaler metric aggregation issue: group-level aggregation suppressed burst-per-connection signals; scaler didn't see hot partitions (validated by comparing per-node serving tokens vs aggregated HA metric).
3) Edge proxy queueing + acceptor backlog amplification: long-lived multiplexed sessions caused uneven distribution of load across acceptors; some acceptors saturated which increased head latency (validated by acceptor queue length histograms).
4) Telemetry blindspot: there was no direct gauge for hedged-request-count per-serving-instance leading to delayed detection.

Contributing factors:
- Legacy partner integration (partner-bETA) had an opt-in that created high rps-per-connection for multiplexing and hit us during their scheduled test window. They were not rate-limited by default.
- Hedges were aggressive for streaming (hedge_multiplier set to 2.0) which is appropriate for model A but not for streaming with long tail responses.
- Autoscaler uses 5m aggregated metrics which masks short 1-2 minute hot spikes.
- No soft circuit-breaker at acceptor level for per-connection request rate.

Short-term mitigations executed (during incident):
- Applied temporary per-tenant rate limit to partner-bETA token group (owner: Priya Nair) -> immediate drop in new session creation.
- Lowered hedge_multiplier for streaming route from 2.0 -> 1.1 (rollbackable) -> reduced duplicate load.
- Manually moved a subset of hot connections to a separate acceptor pool to reduce queue head-of-line blocking.
- Increased alerting sensitivity for hedged-request-rate and acceptor-queue-length to catch earlier.

What worked:
- Targeted tenant throttle and hedge_multiplier reduction visibly reduced load within 3-5 minutes.
- Traces were sufficient to identify duplicate request IDs and confirm hedging amplification.

What didn't work / gaps exposed:
- Autoscaler hysteresis/aggregation hid spike signals. Need finer-grained scaling signals or burst headroom.
- No per-connection circuit breaker leading to head-of-line blocking when a single connection streams many concurrent logical requests.
- Runbook steps for tenant-based emergency throttles were terse; response time slowed as responders debated token groups and quota endpoints.

Follow-up actions (short and medium term) - owners assigned inline: 
- SRE-1 (Jordan Reyes): Add hedged-request-count per-instance metric and dashboard; new alert for sudden hedging amplification (due 2026-06-11).
- SRE-2 (Priya Nair): Update autoscaler to consider 1m bucketed hotness signal and a burst headroom policy (proposal due 2026-06-08, implementation Q3).
- Serving Runtime (Liam O'Connor): Implement per-connection logical-rate circuit breaker at acceptor layer (design doc due 2026-06-15).
- Product/Partner success (Marta Silva): Contact partner-bETA to coordinate improved client-side backoff and announce default tenant rate-limiting rules (owner Marta; contact log and remediation plan due 2026-06-04).
- Oncall docs (Evan Zhou): Expand emergency-runbook steps for tenant-level throttles with exact CLI commands and ticket templates (done 2026-06-04).

Runbook draft (emergency path) - quick checklist for responders:
1) Identify if hedging amplification is present:
   - Query: sum(hedged_requests) by token_group over 1m -> compare to baseline.
   - Look for duplicated request IDs in traces.
2) If a single tenant dominates hedged requests, apply temporary token_group rate limit:
   - Command: infra-cli quota override --tenant <token_group> --rps 20 --window 60s (example)
   - Notify partner and create short-term incident note for CS.
3) Lower hedge multiplier for streaming route (rollbackable):
   - Command: config set routing.streaming.hedge_multiplier=1.1 ; monitor p99
4) If acceptor backlog > 95th percentile for >2m, rehome hot connections to dedicated acceptor pool or enable per-connection circuit breaker if deployed.
5) Escalate to Serving Runtime and Autoscaler owners if autoscaler didn’t add capacity after 90s of sustained >70% per-instance token usage.

Runbook draft (post-incident checks):
- Verify hedged_request metric stabilized for 10m.
- Confirm autoscaler decision log for the period and file a bug if aggregation masked hotness.
- Ensure partner has paused test and has an action plan.
- Run chaos test to simulate high rps-per-connection in staging and ensure circuit breaker activates.

Experiments and proposals (to prevent recurrence):
- Autoscaler fast-path: add a 1m high-watermark signal that can trigger a transient surge pool (small warm pool of spare instances) to absorb 1-5m spikes. (Priya Nair + infra-Q3)
- Hedging adaptivity: make hedge_multiplier route-aware and latency-tail aware (smarter hedging for streaming). Run A/B in prod for three weeks. (Serving Runtime)
- Per-connection token budgeting: enforce logical concurrency limits per multiplexed connection to prevent single-connection hogging. (Design by 2026-06-15)
- Tenant default guardrail: default tenant multiplexing concurrency cap and explicit opt-in for higher concurrency (Product + CS).

On-call takeaways (practical):
- Keep tenant throttle commands bookmarked in SRE runbook Slack channel. Prepared a short cheat-sheet (linked_artifacts above).
- When investigating latency spikes that include hedging, check duplicates in traces early — duplicates are a clear sign of hedging amplification.
- Prefer temporary tenant throttle before global hedge multiplier changes unless tenant unknown.

Communication notes:
- Notified affected customers via status.redwood.com incident page at 18:02 UTC with note: "Degraded streaming and intermittent timeouts in east-1; mitigation in progress."
- Follow-up customer email template (CS): outlined causes, temporary mitigations, and ETA for permanent fixes.

Appendix: Quick diagnostic queries and expected signals (copyable):
- hedged amplification check: sum(rate(api_hedged_requests[1m])) by (token_group)
- acceptor queue backlog: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(acceptor_queue_length_bucket[1m])) by (le,acceptor))
- duplicate request trace finder: trace where request_id repeats && trace.duration > baseline

Raw responder notes (snippets):
- "17:44 - saw a badge of hedged dupes in X-ray. Partner token heavy. Applied token throttle and that made p99 fall almost immediately, so hypothesis validated." - Priya
- "autoscaler looked at aggregated group metric (5m mean) — we need a 1min hotness. I can prototype a delta-based signal this week." - Liam

Status of follow-ups as of last_modified (2026-06-04):
- Emergency runbook expanded with CLI snippets: complete (Evan Zhou).
- Tenant contact and remediation plan: partner responded; agreed to pause tests and implement client-side backoff (Marta Silva).
- Hedged-request metric and dashboard: in progress (Jordan Reyes)
- Autoscaler 1m-bucket proposal: in review (Priya Nair).

Open questions / unresolved risks:
- What is the acceptable transient latency headroom policy before we prefer throttling vs scaling? (proposal needed)
- How will opt-in higher-concurrency tenants be charged or rate-limited in peak windows? (billing/product question)

If you were the next oncall, priorities:
1) Ensure the hedged-request metric alert is firing correctly for 1m windows.
2) Validate the partner has implemented backoff and the tenant throttle is no longer needed.
3) Keep tracking autoscaler prototype progress; if prototype delayed, prepare manual runbook to flip a short-term burst pool.

Document history: initial writeup 2026-05-30 by Jordan Reyes; updates and runbook fragments added through 2026-06-04.

End of field journal.
